enrichment.short_title: Extradition habeas corpus after committal for South African indecent assault charges
key_facts: Godfrey, a British national with South African residence, was requested by South Africa for ten counts of indecent assault alleged at a Randburg nursery school.
He was arrested in the United Kingdom in August 2002 and committed by District Judge Pratt at Bow Street on 17 January 2003.
South Africa was a designated Commonwealth country and an authority to proceed had been issued.
Five counts were unopposed; the applicant challenged sufficiency of evidence on counts 6, 8, 9 and 10, including disputes over bracketed references to 'vagina' in children's statements.
Supporting evidence included police and mothers' accounts of children demonstrating what was alleged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application under section 11 of the Extradition Act 1989 following committal for extradition to South Africa.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 9(8) committal the magistrate must be satisfied that the evidence would be sufficient to require an answer at summary trial; where a child witness's statement, read with supporting evidence, shows indecent touching even if euphemistic language is used, a prima facie case is established and habeas corpus will not lie.
legal_issues: Whether the magistrate had sufficient evidence to commit on the contested indecent assault counts
Whether bracketed anatomical words in children's statements rendered the evidence insufficient or inadmissible
The test under section 9(8) for prima facie case at committal

enrichment.short_title: Tesco fire claim preliminary issues on contract, duty and limitation
key_facts: A serious fire on 4 August 2001 damaged Tesco's Redditch superstore, originally built by Costain in 1989-1990 with architects Peter Hing & Jones (PHJ).
Tesco brought related actions HT-02-07 and HT-02-439 alleging defective fire stopping and inhibiting measures and negligent 1993/1994 inspection reports by Costain.
Tesco later chose to rebuild a larger store rather than reinstate the original building.
The court tried numerous preliminary issues on whether contracts existed, what duties were owed, when causes of action accrued, and whether claims were time-barred.

Costain was held to have entered a 1989 contract by counter-signing Tesco's 20 March 1989 letter, but not on a twelve-year limitation term; tort claims largely accrued at practical completion or on reliance on inspection reports, not at the date of the fire.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of preliminary issues in related actions before the main quantum/liability trial.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues determined; main trial on breach and quantum deferred to a second stage.
enrichment.ratio: Where building defects reduce the value of completed works or where reliance on a negligent inspection report increases remedial cost, a claimant's tort cause of action in economic loss generally accrues when that loss is sustained, not when a later fire occurs; architects do not assume a duty of care to a client or contractor merely by receiving copies of another party's correspondence.
legal_issues: Whether Tesco and Costain made a design-and-build contract in 1989 and on what terms
Whether estoppel or novation extended limitation or contract terms
The scope of Costain's tort duty and duties assumed by inspection letters of October 1993 and May 1994
When Tesco's causes of action accrued for defective construction and negligent inspection
PHJ's contractual and tort duties and whether any duty arose in 1993/1994

enrichment.short_title: BNP poster conviction for religiously aggravated section 5 Public Order offence
key_facts: Norwood, BNP regional organiser for Shropshire, displayed a window poster reading 'Islam out of Britain' and 'Protect the British people', with an image of the burning World Trade Centre and a prohibited crescent and star.
The poster was visible to passers-by from November 2001 until removed by police in January 2002 after a complaint.
He was convicted by District Judge Browning of a religiously aggravated section 5 offence and fined £300.
The poster was found insulting to Muslims, likely to cause alarm or distress, not objectively reasonable, and motivated by religious hostility.
Article 10 was engaged but the section 5 restriction was justified under Article 10(2) and supported by Article 17.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Oswestry Magistrates' Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrate's conviction and findings upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 5 prosecution requires proof of insulting display, awareness or intent, and likelihood of harassment, alarm or distress; where a poster attacks Muslim followers rather than merely criticising religion, and is religiously aggravated, Article 10 does not require acquittal because the objective unreasonableness of the conduct aligns with the statutory offence once the prosecution proves the section 5 limbs.
legal_issues: Whether the poster was threatening, abusive or insulting and likely to cause alarm or distress
Whether the offence was religiously aggravated under sections 28 and 31
Whether conviction was compatible with Article 10 freedom of expression
The structure of section 5 and the role of the section 5(3) reasonableness defence
Whether the reverse burden in section 5(3) must be read down to an evidential burden

enrichment.short_title: Bill of lading incorporation of London arbitration and anti-suit injunction

statutes_considered.title: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1992

key_facts: Welex, consignee of steel plates damaged on the Epsilon Rosa, arrested the vessel in Portugal and began proceedings in Poland against Rosa and Alexia Navigation.
A voyage charter recap telex agreed London arbitration and English law; a Congenbill bill of lading incorporated charterparty terms including the law and arbitration clause.
David Steel J held the arbitration clause incorporated and granted a permanent anti-suit injunction restraining Polish proceedings.
Welex argued loss of Portuguese security if forced to arbitrate in London and that it had not negotiated the clause.
Rosa admitted liability in London arbitration; the dispute concerned pre-shipment damage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against Commercial Court decisions on incorporation and anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; incorporation and anti-suit injunction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A broker recap telex together with standard charter terms can constitute the charterparty incorporated into a Congenbill bill of lading where terms are readily ascertainable; a party suing in a non-contractual forum must show strong reasons to escape an exclusive arbitration agreement, and self-induced delay in commencing arbitration weakens a security-based objection.
legal_issues: Whether London arbitration terms in a recap telex and/or executed charterparty were incorporated into the bill of lading
Whether the court had jurisdiction to grant a final anti-suit injunction
Whether strong reasons existed to permit Polish proceedings despite the arbitration clause
The effect of Brussels/Lugano and New York Convention considerations on anti-suit relief

enrichment.short_title: Wrong-address dawn raid and malicious procurement of search warrant
key_facts: During Operation Trotter into armed robberies, police obtained section 26 Theft Act warrants to search 19 New Henderson Street and 27 South Hill Road for stolen cash linked to suspect Dean Metcalfe.
The Keegan family had occupied 19 New Henderson Street since April 1999, before the robberies, but police believed Metcalfe was linked to the address from electoral roll and prior stops.
At 7 a.m. on 21 October 1999 officers forcibly entered the Keegans' home; the mistake was quickly recognised and the search abandoned within fifteen minutes.
The county court judge found no malice in procuring the warrant and that entry pursuant to the warrant and section 17 PACE was lawful.
The Court of Appeal held there was no reasonable and probable cause for the warrant but malice was not proved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimants' appeal to the Court of Appeal from Birkenhead County Court judgment for the Chief Constable.
enrichment.ratio: Malicious procurement of a search warrant requires improper motive, not mere negligence or inadequate enquiries; absence of reasonable and probable cause does not alone establish malice, and execution of a valid warrant or lawful section 17 entry protects officers even where intelligence linking a suspect to premises was mistaken.
legal_issues: Whether police lacked reasonable and probable cause to apply for the search warrant
Whether malice in procuring the warrant was established
Whether forcible entry amounted to trespass
The ingredients of the tort in Gibbs v Rea and the mental element of malice
Whether section 17(2)(a) PACE permits belief that a person 'may be' on premises

enrichment.short_title: Procedure to challenge mediated settlement after software marketing dispute
key_facts: Jacob J found Vedatech entitled to reasonable remuneration for marketing software in Japan for Crystal Decisions; the parties mediated and signed a settlement with an entire agreement clause in August 2002.
Vedatech later sought to rescind or challenge the settlement for alleged fraud in the Japanese subsidiary accounts and other grounds.
Jacob J stayed the existing proceedings, required new proceedings to challenge the settlement, and ordered Vedatech to pay £4,000 costs.
Defendants issued fresh proceedings for a declaration that the settlement was enforceable while the stay remained.
By a majority the Court of Appeal set aside the costs order but upheld the stay and allowed the new proceedings to continue rather than lift the stay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from case management orders made by Jacob J after mediation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: no order as to costs below; otherwise appeal dismissed and stay maintained by majority.
enrichment.ratio: A party may challenge a settlement agreement for fraud or other vitiating factors within existing proceedings rather than as a matter of law being required to commence fresh proceedings; however, where new proceedings have already been issued and a stay imposed, the court may exercise its discretion to let the new action determine validity, especially where both routes are procedurally available.
legal_issues: Whether fraud or rescission claims had to be brought in fresh proceedings
Whether Jacob J's stay was a proper case management order
Whether the £4,000 costs order should stand
Whether commencing fresh proceedings while an appeal was pending was an abuse of process

confidence.notes: Full procedural judgment with split court on stay but clear outcome on costs and majority disposition.

enrichment.short_title: Pre-action disclosure of KPMG files in solicitors' negligence claim
key_facts: Moresfield and the Swifts sold Kenal shares to Hillbridge in 1998; a shortfall mechanism in the share sale agreement led to agreed deductions after dispute.
They sued their solicitors Banners for negligent drafting; Banners threatened a contribution claim against Kenal's auditors KPMG.
KPMG had voluntarily offered mutual pre-action disclosure in March 2002 but withdrew after proceedings began and no Part 20 claim was issued.
Banners applied under CPR 31.16 and alternatively 31.17 for KPMG's two transaction files before trial fixed for November 2003.
Collins J ordered disclosure, finding the parties may well be future litigants and the files likely relevant to retainer, advice and alleged assurances on shortfall.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery application for pre-action or non-party disclosure against accountants in ongoing professional negligence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted for pre-action disclosure of KPMG's two files under CPR 31.16.
enrichment.ratio: Pre-action disclosure under CPR 31.16 may be ordered where the respondent may well be a party to anticipated contribution proceedings, standard disclosure would cover focused files, and disclosure is likely to assist resolution or save costs; a prior voluntary disclosure offer is a relevant discretionary factor even if not binding.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 31.16 conditions were satisfied for disclosure against a non-party likely to be sued
Whether CPR 31.17 provided an alternative basis for disclosure in the main action
Whether delay and absence of a Part 20 claim barred pre-action disclosure
Whether KPMG's files were likely to support Banners' defence or contribution claim

enrichment.short_title: Private hire operator use of hackney carriages after consent declaration
key_facts: Shanks challenged North Tyneside Council licensing conditions by judicial review and related magistrates' court proceedings.
The parties reached consent terms including a declaration that a private hire vehicle operator is not precluded from using hackney carriages for private hiring.
The claimants withdrew their magistrates' court complaint and gave an undertaking as part of the settlement.
Mackay J held the claimants had substantially achieved their objective and ordered the council to pay their High Court costs, assessable in Newcastle if agreed.
No order was made as to magistrates' court costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative Court costs ruling following consent settlement of judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration made by consent; defendants ordered to pay claimants' High Court costs; no order as to magistrates' court costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where judicial review settles by consent on terms that give claimants the licensing clarification they sought, costs may still be awarded against a public authority defendant despite sensible late settlement, especially where the dispute was a pure legal point that could have been resolved earlier.

enrichment.short_title: Warsaw Convention Article 17 and deep vein thrombosis on ordinary flights
key_facts: Group litigation by passengers alleging DVT and pulmonary embolism caused by long-haul air travel against major international airlines.
Claims were brought under Article 17 of the Warsaw Convention as incorporated by the Carriage by Air Act 1961.
A specimen matrix assumed symptomatic DVT caused by the flight, industry-standard seating and cabin conditions, and carrier knowledge of increased DVT risk without warnings.
Nelson J held the matrix disclosed no 'accident' within Article 17; passengers appealed.
The Court of Appeal held normal flight conditions and failures to warn were not events or accidents under the Saks definition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from preliminary issue decision in group litigation.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 17 of the Warsaw Convention, liability requires an accident—an unexpected or unusual external event—not mere injury from the normal operation of the aircraft; permanent cabin features of an ordinary flight and omissions to warn or advise cannot constitute such an event, because inaction is a non-event.
legal_issues: The meaning of 'accident' in Article 17 of the Warsaw Convention
Whether cramped seating and normal cabin conditions can be an accident
Whether failure to warn of DVT risk constitutes an accident
Application of Air France v Saks and distinction from Husain v Olympic Airways

enrichment.short_title: Building contract bay windows, inconvenience damages and costs set-off
key_facts: Builder Willers sued neighbours the Boyntons for balance due on home extension works under a July 1991 quotation totalling £53,460 plus additional works.
The Boyntons counterclaimed for remedial works for defective workmanship and inconvenience during rectification over several years.
The judge held bay window construction was excluded from the original quotation because the parties had not finalised bay design; remedial damages for bays were limited to £500 plus VAT.
General damages for inconvenience were assessed at £500; net judgment for the builder was £3,910 plus interest after set-off.
The judge awarded the builder costs on an indemnity basis from mid-trial after encouraging settlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendants' appeal to the Court of Appeal from Sheffield County Court after ten-day trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all three grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Where a fixed-price quotation and drawings omit major bay construction and evidence shows the parties had not agreed bay design, bay works are excluded from the quoted price and rectification damages are limited accordingly; a modest inconvenience award will not be disturbed without reliable evidence, and set-off of counterclaim damages does not require a separate costs split where claim and counterclaim issues overlap.
legal_issues: Whether construction and installation of bay windows was included in the quoted contract price
Whether general damages for inconvenience were too low
Whether the judge erred in awarding overall costs to the successful builder after set-off
Construction of quotation items referring to windows 'as per drawing'

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment addressing all three appeal grounds with detailed contract construction analysis.
